_why_a_separate_file: Same reason as chaindrop_elastic_2026_08.json: one source, one file, so a claim can be
attributed, scored and contradicted. StepSecurity is the deepest technical teardown of
this campaign published so far and is the only source for the pre-publish GitHub
timeline, the token-revocation monitor, the runner-memory scrape and the self-republish
chain. Merging it would destroy the provenance that makes §1.2 arbitration possible.
The hunt queries the union of all source files; it reports the arbitrated verdict set.

Campaign footprint: StepSecurity states 444 packages / 2,212 versions as of 2026-08-04 18:10 UTC, and 433 packages / 2,201 versions for the second wave alone. Consistent with SafeDep and Cloudsmith, higher than JFrog. Still a floor, not a count - see §1.4.
_relationship_to_shai_hulud_2026_08.note: Silence is not denial. An indicator absent here is unclaimed by StepSecurity, not refuted by it, and stays in hunt scope on the other source's assertion.

setup.mjs_v1.role: First-wave dropper. Larger because it carries the full Bun bootstrap inline.

setup.mjs_v2.role: Second-wave dropper, trimmed. Two sizes for one filename - another reason filename hunting is worthless here.

stage2.role: Credential collector. Same bytes under two names.

bun_bootstrap.post_download: chmod 755, execute stage 2, then delete the staging directory
_why_this_is_the_chokepoint: The dropper carries no payload. It fetches Bun from github.com over HTTPS, and the
payload only runs under Bun. An egress allowlist that does not include the GitHub
release CDN stops the chain at its first hop - stage 2 never executes and no
credential is ever read. This is the single highest-value preventive control in the
campaign, and it is cheaper than blocking C2 because it is one origin, not 75.
Blocking github.com wholesale is not the ask; the ask is that build agents fetch
release binaries through a controlled mirror.

persistence.redundancy: The two sets cross-reference each other. Removing one leaves the other live, and opening the repository in either tool re-executes the chain with no npm install involved.

token_monitor.behavior: Polls https://api.github.com/user every 60 seconds for 24 hours and fires the payload when the token stops authenticating.
_operational_consequence: This inverts the standard IR order. Revoking the stolen token is the trigger
condition, not the remediation: the monitor treats revocation as the signal to
re-run collection and re-exfiltrate from whatever credentials are still live.
The monitor must be removed from every affected host BEFORE the first revocation.
It is also a persistence mechanism that survives cleanup of setup.mjs, math_init.js,
.claude/ and .vscode/ entirely - none of those paths contain it.

ethereum.behavior: Tries 75 public Ethereum RPC endpoints in sequence until one returns the current C2 address.

exfil.healthcheck: GET /router, which deliberately returns 400 or 404 so the host looks broken to a casual probe

_domain_blocking_is_insufficient: Blocking npm-cache.com removes the primary exfil channel and is worth doing. It does
not sever control: the address is resolved on chain at runtime, and where the
blockchain read also fails the worm falls back to GitHub commit search. Three
independent channels. The RPC providers and the Bun fetch are the chokepoints.

exfil_envelope.chain: gzip(JSON) -> AES-256-GCM -> RSA-OAEP-SHA256 wrapped key -> base64 -> POST
exfil_envelope.bidirectional: A response containing a `code` field is passed to eval(). The channel is not exfil-only; it is remote code execution back into the victim.
exfil_envelope._consequence: A host that reached npm-cache.com cannot be scoped as 'credentials stolen'. It must be scoped as 'attacker had arbitrary code execution for the duration of the connection'.

aws.signing: SigV4, requests signed with any harvested key

credential_targets.kubernetes: kubeconfig discovery plus service-account token theft

runner_memory_scrape.technique: A sudo python3 helper reads /proc/<Runner.Worker pid>/mem and greps for "isSecret":true
_consequence: This defeats masked-secret hygiene entirely. A secret never written to a log or a
file is still in the runner process's heap, and any job with passwordless sudo on a
self-hosted runner can read it. It affects every secret the runner has ever handled
in that job, not just the ones the compromised step referenced.
Scope: self-hosted Linux runners only. GitHub-hosted runners are discarded per job,
and the estate's runners cxdkrprdapp12-17.comfort.com are exactly in scope.

self_republish.tarball_handling: Recomputes SHA-512 and SHA-1 so the repacked tarball passes integrity checks
self_republish.provenance: Self-mints Sigstore attestations via fulcio.sigstore.dev and rekor.sigstore.dev
_provenance_is_not_a_defence: Two independent paths defeat provenance in this campaign. First, the attacker mints
its own Sigstore attestation from the compromised publisher context. Second - and
worse - the first-wave publish went out through the project's own legitimate release
workflow, so keyv@6.0.0 carries genuine, valid SLSA provenance attesting that it was
built from the jaredwray/keyv repository at a real commit. It was. The commit was
malicious. Provenance proves build integrity, not source integrity, and a control
that verifies provenance would have passed this package.

github_abuse.workflow_behaviour: Writes ${{ toJSON(secrets) }} to format-results.txt and uploads it as an artifact
github_abuse.exfil_staging_repos: Repositories created under the victim account holding results-*.json
_variant_not_contradiction: shai_hulud_2026_08.json records the exfil workflow as codeql_analysis.yml with a
StepSecurity records it as a workflow named 'Run Copilot'. These are two observed
variants of the same primitive - dump toJSON(secrets) into a file, upload the file -
not conflicting claims. Detect on the primitive: a workflow file added by a
non-human identity that references toJSON(secrets). Detecting on either filename
misses the other variant and the next one.

pre_publish_timeline_utc._provenance: StepSecurity is the only source for this sequence. Single-source, unverified against Tier 0 - the commits are in a third-party repository we do not control and cannot query as ground truth. High value: it shows the compromise began 33 minutes before the first malicious publish, which is the only part of the campaign where detection was still possible.

events.event: Account compromise. Commit ee2681a to jaredwray/keyv main adds the dropper, adds "preinstall": "node setup.mjs", adds the dropper to the package `files` array, adds a fake cover test at core/keyv/test/preinstall.test.ts, and modifies scripts/release-publish.ts to read `latestMajor` from the repository's own package.json instead of an environment variable.
First malicious publish, @keyv/mongo@6.0.0. Tier 0 confirmed - see supply-chain-hunt-ttp.md §1.3.
keyv@6.0.0 published by the project's own legitimate release workflow, with valid SLSA provenance. Tier 0 confirmed.
Second wave. 433 packages / 2,201 versions from stolen publish tokens. Close time disputed - see contradicts[] above.

_release_tooling_hijack: The release-publish.ts edit is the mechanism, and it is the most reusable technique in
the campaign. Moving latestMajor out of a protected CI variable and into a file the
attacker already controls means the malicious major publishes as `latest` through the
project's real, signed, provenance-emitting release pipeline. Nothing in the pipeline
was compromised. It did exactly what its configuration told it to.
Detection surface: a diff to release or publish tooling that relocates a version or
channel decision from CI configuration into repository-controlled state. That is a
reviewable event in a pull request, and it is upstream of every downstream indicator

second_wave_namespaces._use: Input to the Tier 0 re-derivation that resolves the 12:11 vs 13:20 disagreement, and to the §1.4 full-campaign scope expansion.

totals_claimed.note: A snapshot of a spreading worm. Treat as a floor.

locale_kill_switch.behavior: Reads the LANG environment variable and exits without executing if it indicates a Russian locale.
_hunting_consequence: This is a false-negative source, not just trivia. A host with a Russian locale returns
clean from every behavioral rule in the detection set - no Bun spawn, no stage 2, no
C2 - while the dropper is on disk and would have run. The file-hash rules still fire;
the process and network rules do not. Any zero from a behavioral rule must be paired
with a locale check before it is read as clean. Consistent with CIS-based operator
avoidance of domestic prosecution, which is an attribution hint and nothing more.

mitigations_recommended: npm ci --ignore-scripts in CI, always. Never npm install.
Egress allowlist on build agents. Blocks the Bun fetch at the first hop, so stage 2 never runs.

Package-manager-native release-age gate: npm 11.10+ min-release-age, pnpm 10.16+ minimumReleaseAge, Yarn 4.10+ npmMinimalAgeGate, Bun 1.3+ minimumReleaseAge, Dependabot cooldown. Every malicious version in this campaign was unpublished within hours; a 24-72h gate makes the entire window a non-event without a registry proxy.
Branch protection plus required commit signing on release-critical repositories. The pre-publish sequence was four unsigned commits to main.
Remove the token monitor from every affected host before revoking any credential.
hunting_notes: Hunt the two setup.mjs variants by hash, not by name or size. Same filename, 29,918 and 11,017 bytes, both malicious - and legitimate setup.mjs files exist in many repositories.
The Bun fetch is a better detection than the C2 contact: one origin, no on-chain indirection, and it happens before any credential is read. It needs RemoteUrl, so it needs Network Protection.

Runner-memory scraping is invisible to file and network telemetry. Hunt it as a process pattern - python3 under sudo with /proc in the command line, initiated from a runner work directory - and only on self-hosted runners.
The token monitor is the only artifact that survives a clean-up of setup.mjs, math_init.js, .claude/ and .vscode/. Sweep for it separately, and before revocation.
A host that reached npm-cache.com had inbound eval() available to the attacker. Scope it as arbitrary code execution, not as credential theft.
